## Big Question {.role-slide}

Do linguistic objects form recurring groups when the group labels are not supplied to the analysis?

## Data {.role-slide}

A [unit of analysis](../../foundations/linguistic-data.html) may be a speaker represented by language-use ratings, a vowel token represented by F1 and F2, or a language represented by grammatical features.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

The rows, features, scaling, distance, and candidate number of groups all help determine the structure that can be found.

## This Module {.role-slide .compact}

1. Construct the representation and geometry.
2. Fit and evaluate K-means clustering.
3. Replace centroids with Gaussian component distributions.
4. Evaluate mixture specifications on held-out speakers.

## Finding unobserved groups {.section-slide}

Two statistical representations

## Possibility {.role-slide}

K-means assigns every object to the nearest centroid. A [**finite mixture model**](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html) gives every object a model-based probability for each component.

<div class="source">Stan User’s Guide, Finite mixtures</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

A learned group is a property of the representation and fitted procedure. It is not automatically a linguistic category.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/index.html)

## Representing objects for clustering {.section-slide}

Rows define what can be grouped

## Data {.role-slide}

Three speakers have English and Spanish speaking ratings:

$$
\mathbf X=
\begin{bmatrix}
5&1\\
4&2\\
1&5
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

## Method {.role-slide}

Each row is one speaker. The two columns define similarity. Identifiers and variables reserved for interpretation remain outside the feature matrix.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Numerical storage does not guarantee numerical meaning. Coding language names as 1, 2, and 3 creates an unsupported ordered geometry.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/representing-objects.html)

## Distance and scaling {.section-slide}

Defining the geometry

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Euclidean distance**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14) combines squared column differences.

$$
d(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=
\sqrt{\sum_m(x_{im}-x_{jm})^2}
$$

<div class="source">Penn State STAT 505</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Challenge {.role-slide}

A difference of 1,000 tokens dominates a difference of one rating point before scaling. Changing token units can therefore change the learned geometry.

## Approach {.role-slide}

Standardization expresses each difference in observed standard-deviation units. During validation, estimate means and standard deviations from training rows only.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Equal observed variance does not imply equal reliability or theoretical importance. Euclidean distance remains a linguistic assumption about comparable differences.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.html)

## K-means clustering {.section-slide}

Alternating assignments and centroid updates

## Method {.role-slide}

[**K-means clustering**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14) minimizes the within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances.

$$
W=\sum_i\lVert\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_{z_i}\rVert^2
$$

<div class="source">Penn State STAT 505</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Implementation {.role-slide .compact}

1. Assign every row to its nearest centroid.
2. Replace each centroid with the mean of its assigned rows.
3. Repeat until assignments no longer change.

## Question {.role-slide}

For points $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$ in one cluster, why is the updated centroid $(0,1)$?

## Upshot {.role-slide}

K-means can converge to a [**local minimum**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14). Compare the fitted loss over several initializations.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/k-means.html)

## Within-cluster loss {.section-slide}

Comparing candidate values of K

## Surprising Fact {.role-slide}

Training within-cluster loss cannot increase when another centroid is added. More centroids can reproduce the earlier solution and may improve it.

## Method {.role-slide}

An [**elbow plot**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14) displays fitted within-cluster loss against $K$. The elbow method looks for diminishing reductions.

<div class="source">Penn State STAT 505</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

An elbow may be ambiguous and depends on representation, scaling, distance, and initialization. Training compactness does not establish held-out performance.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.html)

## Silhouette widths {.section-slide}

Cohesion relative to separation

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**silhouette width**](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/cluster/html/silhouette.html) compares average within-cluster distance $a(i)$ with distance to the nearest alternative cluster $b(i)$.

<div class="source">R cluster reference</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/cluster/html/silhouette.html
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

$$
s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}.
$$

Positive values favor the assigned cluster. Negative values favor a neighboring cluster.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Silhouette widths diagnose compact separation under the chosen distance. They do not establish that the groups are linguistic categories.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/silhouette-scores.html)

## Validation without outcome labels {.section-slide}

Predicting held-out rows

## Question {.role-slide}

Without observed group labels, what can a clustering predict for a row omitted during fitting?

## Answer {.role-slide}

Assign the held-out row to its nearest training centroid and record its squared distance to that centroid as predictive loss.

## Implementation {.role-slide .compact}

1. Estimate scaling from training rows.
2. Fit candidate centroids to those rows.
3. Transform held-out rows with training scaling.
4. Compare paired nearest-centroid losses.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Lower loss establishes better numerical prediction under the declared geometry. It does not establish recovery of an unobserved linguistic category.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/unsupervised-validation.html)

## Gaussian mixtures {.section-slide}

Overlapping component distributions

## Data {.role-slide}

Peterson and Barney measured F1 and F2 for vowel tokens in an /hVd/ frame. Intended vowel labels remain outside the mixture fit.

<div class="source">Peterson and Barney 1952; phonTools pb52</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
2. https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

A [**Gaussian mixture model (GMM)**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html) combines weighted Gaussian component densities.

$$
p(\mathbf x_i)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i;\boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma_k)
$$

<div class="source">scikit-learn, Gaussian mixture models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

Each [covariance matrix](../../random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.html) controls component spread and orientation. Every component contributes density to every token.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

A covariance can collapse around very few observations and produce an unbounded likelihood. A tiny fitted component may therefore be a numerical failure.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

A component is a distributional summary under the chosen representation. It is not automatically a phoneme or intended vowel category.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.html)

## Posterior membership {.section-slide}

Normalizing component contributions

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [**posterior probability of component membership**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html) applies [Bayes’ rule](../../foundations/bayes-rule.html):

$$
\Pr(Z_i=k\mid\mathbf x_i)=
\frac{\pi_kp(\mathbf x_i\mid Z_i=k)}{\sum_h\pi_hp(\mathbf x_i\mid Z_i=h)}.
$$

<div class="source">scikit-learn, Gaussian mixture models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

These probabilities, often called responsibilities, sum to one for each token. A hard assignment discards the remaining membership uncertainty.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

[**Label switching**](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html) means that component numbers have no stable linguistic identity across separate fits.

<div class="source">Stan User’s Guide, Finite mixtures</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/posterior-membership.html)

## Expectation-maximization {.section-slide}

Fitting a Gaussian mixture

## Method {.role-slide}

The [**expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html) alternates conditional expectations of component labels with parameter updates.

<div class="source">scikit-learn, Gaussian mixture models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## Implementation {.role-slide .compact}

1. Compute responsibilities under provisional parameters.
2. Update weights, means, and covariances with responsibility-weighted quantities.
3. Repeat until the fitted objective stabilizes.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Expectation-maximization finds a local solution. Use several starts and inspect nearly empty or collapsing components.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/expectation-maximization.html)

## Choosing a mixture with BIC {.section-slide}

Comparing declared specifications

## Question {.role-slide}

How should component count and covariance structure be compared without choosing the specification with the largest fitted likelihood automatically?

## Method {.role-slide}

The [**Bayesian information criterion**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html), introduced on the earlier [information-criteria page](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.html), adds a parameter-count penalty to maximized likelihood.

$$
\mathrm{BIC}=-2\ell(\widehat\theta)+k\log n
$$

<div class="source">scikit-learn, Gaussian mixture models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

BIC selects among declared candidate distributions for the measured data. It does not establish a true number of linguistic categories.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture.html)

## Validating a mixture on held-out speakers {.section-slide}

Predictive density for absent speakers

## Method {.role-slide}

For a held-out token, use log loss

$$
L_i(M)=-\log p_M(\mathbf x_i\mid D_{\mathrm{train}}).
$$

Lower loss means higher fitted predictive density.

## Implementation {.role-slide .compact}

1. Hold out every token from each test speaker.
2. Estimate scaling and the complete mixture inside training data.
3. Return token losses to held-out speakers.
4. Examine stability across starts and speaker splits.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Held-out speaker loss evaluates density for absent speakers under the stated normalization information. It remains conditional on the candidate set and representation.

[Return to the notes](../../latent-structure/validating-a-mixture.html)

## Conclusion {.section-slide}

Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data

## Big Question {.role-slide}

Do linguistic objects form recurring groups when the group labels are not supplied to the analysis?

## Answer {.role-slide .compact}

1. State what each row and feature represents.
2. Treat scaling and distance as modeling assumptions.
3. Separate fitted components from linguistic categories.
4. Match held-out evaluation to the sampling unit in the claim.
